sections.body: The AI Economist covers the places where machine learning has moved from research papers into the daily machinery of money. Forecasting the economy now leans on large panels of indicators and text, quantitative trading runs on models that retrain as markets move, and credit desks score borrowers with data that goes well beyond a traditional credit file. Private equity teams use models to screen targets and draft diligence questions, while portfolio managers use them to size positions and test scenarios. Reading the market's language means turning earnings calls, filings and news into signals, and alternative data means card transactions, satellite imagery and shipping records. Agent workflows put software between the analyst and the trade, and crypto markets apply the same techniques to a market that never closes. Governance and fiduciary risk sit over all of it, because someone still has to answer for the decision.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The parts that work are narrow and measurable. Short horizon forecasting and pattern detection in liquid markets are genuinely useful, and document processing in credit and diligence saves real analyst hours. The parts that do not work are the promises of general economic prediction, and the honest limits are regime change, thin data and feedback loops where everyone acting on the same signal erases it. Backtests overstate results because they cannot reproduce the slippage, crowding and capacity of live trading. In credit and private markets, models inherit the biases of past lending and past deals, and they struggle where history is short. Governance is the least settled area, since rules on model use, disclosure and accountability are still being written and enforced unevenly across jurisdictions.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The section is built as a chain from data to decision to accountability. Macroeconomic Econometrics and Reading the Market's Language cover the inputs, one from official statistics and one from text, and Alternative Data extends that input set to non traditional sources. Quantitative Trading and Crypto Markets and Decentralised Finance show the techniques applied in fast, liquid settings, while Fixed Income and Credit Risk and Private Equity and Deal Sourcing show them in slower, negotiated ones. Portfolio Construction sits above the trading pages as the place where signals become positions and risk budgets. Agent Workflows in Finance describes how these pieces get stitched into automated processes, and Governance and Fiduciary Risk closes the section by asking who is responsible when the process is wrong. A reader new to the field should start with the two input pages, then follow the chain in order.
